newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: U.S./France shape up for trade war in Africa.
newsitem.headline: U.S./France shape up for trade war in Africa.

text.p: France and the United States are shaping up for a battle for business supremacy in West and Central Africa, business analysts say.
The stakes are getting larger with governments in the region privatising everything from oilpalm plantations to telephone and railway networks.
Also at stake are the multi-sector contracts totalling more than $3.5 billion a year distributed by the African Development Bank (AfDB), foreign trade representatives say.
"There are great business opportunities in Africa and at the African Development Bank," AfDB's U.S. Executive Director Alice Dear told a U.S. business mission at the Abidjan-based bank.

"We want to ensure that U.S. companies are informed about business opportunities at the bank and in Africa and that they have a level playing field in competing in international bidding opportunities for bank-financed projects," she said this week.
U.S. companies won 8.14 percent of AfDB contracts in 1995, compared with 11.85 percent for the French.

The U.S. mission of 40 business leaders from 25 firms in all sectors, arrived in Ivory Coast after touring Congo and Equatorial Guinea, where Boston-based United Meridian Corp and Mobil Corp are in joint oil exploration.
A French trade mission was in Ivory Coast in December.
The skirmishing between France and the United States has already started in West and Central Africa where the French have dominated historically.

"Americans rejected in favour of the French," headlined an opposition daily in Ivory Coast this month after authorities disqualified a local consortium allied to U.S. giant AT&T from bidding for the state phone company.
Debate is still raging after that decision, which left France Telecom as favourite to clinch the deal for CI-TELCOM, whose value is estimated at up to $350 million.
The appointment of Ghana's Kofi Annan thwarted France's bid to ensure a Francophone African succeeded Boutros Boutros-Ghali as U.N. chief last month.

In the field of trade, the scales are tipped in its favour because of strong historic and economic ties to the region. Thirteen states are linked by the French language and the common CFA franc currency which is backed by the French treasury.
French companies understand the local culture and have generally stayed during the hard times when others have cut and run.

Ivory Coast is regarded in Paris as the crown jewel of France's former African colonies and French firms have had it virtually to themselves. They have been best placed to take over privatised state firms. For example, engineering group Bouygues SA has since built up huge stakes in energy and utilities.
French exports to the country in the first six months of 1996 amounted to $457 million compared with $173 million for the United States for the whole of 1995, official figures show.
U.S. investment in Francophone Africa has been constrained in the past by language and cultural problems and lack of information on opportunities, American officials say.

"They have in the past focused on markets which are attractive in placing capital, such as Latin America and Asia," one said. "Companies that are here are very sophisticated and tend to examine very closely whether to go into a deal or not."
Times are changing. The Americans have had a long history in oil, notably in Nigeria and Angola, dating back to the 1960s.
Now U.S. firms are seeking to expand investment in oil, energy and telecommunications in traditionally French domains.
United Meridian is the only firm producing oil in Ivory Coast. It is in consortium with Shell Exploration Africa BV for a costly deep-water search off Ivory Coast.
Two of Ivory Coast's three cellular networks are U.S.-owned.

This week Congo chose Atlantic Tele-Network Inc, which is based in U.S. Virgin Islands, as operator for its national phone network in a $42.5 million deal. Niger issued a cellular licence to U.S.-owned Telecel International, which already has franchises in Zaire, Rwanda and Ivory Coast.
